stories.title: KENYA: Bishops Decry Curbs on Free Speech, Urge Respect for Places of Worship
stories.description:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
Catholic Bishops in Kenya have raised concern over the growing attacks on freedom of expression ahead of the 2027 General Election, condemning continued abductions, enforced disappearances and harassment of critics, some of them allegedly carried out with police involvement.
In the same breath, the Bishops banned politicians from addressing congregations in Catholic churches anywhere in the country, saying places of worship must not be turned into campaign podiums.
The Church leaders made the remarks on Thursday, November 12, during their four-day plenary assembly in Embu Diocese.
The Bishops said free speech in Kenya is being tested “on all fronts” and is frequently violated as political temperatures rise ahead of the polls.
They defended the constitutional right of civil society to raise issues of national importance, the right of journalists to practise freely, and the right of human rights defenders to speak out, but noted with concern that people exercising these rights continue to be abducted, made to disappear, or harassed.
Of greater worry, they said, are cases in which armed individuals work hand in hand with police officers, and others where police stand by as hired goons attack people expressing their views lawfully.
“We, the Catholic Bishops, condemn violations of freedom of expression and association,” the statement read.
The Prelates under their umbrella body, the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops (KCCB), said Kenyans must be allowed to enjoy their freedoms as an essential part of building a vibrant democracy. They, however, cautioned that freedom comes with responsibility, urging citizens to steer clear of inciting, spiteful, tribal, hateful, or demeaning remarks.
They also called on security agencies to apply the law without bias, warning against favouring any candidate or political party.
In their Thursday press briefing, the Bishops said election season does not give anyone licence to convert sacred spaces into political arenas. Quoting Habakkuk 2:20, which calls on all the earth to keep silent before God in His holy temple, they reminded Kenyans that churches deserve the highest reverence.
They noted that people from all walks of life, including supporters of rival political parties, come to church as worshippers seeking inner peace, not as partisans. While everyone remains welcome, the Bishops said some politicians have been attempting to exploit church gatherings to campaign.
The Bishops directed that no political address shall be given in any Catholic church across the country, and instructed priests to enforce the position “with diligence and the seriousness it deserves.” Priests, they said, have a pastoral duty to shield sacred places from campaign activity.
Politicians, they added, have plenty of other avenues to reach voters, including the media, public barazas and roadside rallies, and should leave churches as places of unity, love and care open to all regardless of political affiliation.

stories.title: KENYA: Pope Appoints Augustinian Priest as Coadjutor Bishop of Kenya’s Kisii Diocese
stories.description:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
On Friday, November 13, Pope Leo XIV appointed Fr. Joseph Onyango Oduor, a member of the Order of Saint Augustine (O.S.A.), as Coadjutor Bishop of Kenya’s Catholic Diocese of Kisii.
As Coadjutor Bishop, Monsignor Oduor will assist the current Bishop of Kisii, Rt. Rev. Joseph Mairura Okemwa, in the pastoral governance of the diocese and holds the automatic right to succeed him when the See falls vacant.”
In a letter to priests, religious and the laity on Monday, November 10, Bishop Okemwa had disclosed that he had requested an assistant to support him in the mission, saying, “I asked for a helper in the Episcopate work in the Diocese, of which my request has been answered.”
Until his appointment, Msgr. Oduor was serving as parish priest of St Monica Parish in Nyamsaria, within the Archdiocese of Kisumu.
He joined the Augustinian Order in Kenya in 1998, pursued philosophical studies at the Consolata Institute of Philosophy and theological studies at Tangaza University, both in Nairobi, before proceeding to Jos, Nigeria, for his novitiate. He later earned a Licentiate in Philosophy from the Catholic University of Eastern Africa (CUEA) in Nairobi.
The Bishop-elect professed his perpetual vows on October 16, 2005, and was ordained a priest a year later, on November 4, 2006.  He began his priestly ministry at Sacred Heart Parish in Baba Dogo, Nairobi, where he served as parish vicar from 2006 to 2009 before taking over as parish priest until 2011.
He then spent seven years shaping future Augustinian priests as Prior and Formator at the order's International Formation House, the Theologicum, in Nairobi, between 2012 and 2019. In 2020, he was then posted to St Monica Parish in Nyamsaria, Kisumu.
During his time in the Archdiocese of Kisumu, he also served as Dean of the Kisumu Deanery from 2021 to 2024, and has been a member of the archdiocese's College of Consultors since 2024.
Within his religious order, he has served as an advisor to the Vicariate of the Augustinians in Kenya since 2015.
When the announcement was made public at the Holy Mass that was held at the Cathedral to welcome the Coadjutor Bishop, he addressed the congregation and pledged obedience and communion, noting that he would serve the diocese in humility.
“I stand here with humility and obedience as I give thanks and praise to Almighty God for calling me through the appointment of the Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV, to be part of you,” he said.
Drawing inspiration from the Virgin Mary’s response at the Annunciation, the Bishop-elect said he had wholeheartedly embraced God’s will for his life and ministry.
He thanked Bishop Okemwa for the warm welcome and a fatherly embrace, and promised to work closely with him in the mission of evangelization.
“Your Lordship, I promise to work in obedience and in communion with you, with the Holy Father, and indeed in collaboration with all the clergy, religious men and women, and all the faithful of the diocese,” he said.
The Bishop-elect expressed special gratitude to Pope Leo XIV for entrusting him with the responsibility of serving the people of God in Kisii, and to Monsignor Luciano Labanca, Chargé d’Affaires of the Apostolic Nunciature in Kenya, for communicating the appointment and accompanying him in the days leading up to the announcement.
He also thanked the priests, religious sisters and brothers, and Christians who had travelled from different parts of the diocese for the ceremony, as well as all those involved in preparing for the occasion.
The Bishop-elect was accompanied by his religious superior, Fr Robert Karanja Ileri, who represented the Order of Saint Augustine at the event.

stories.title: UGANDA: Family Must Take a Leading Role in Holistic Formation of Children, says Prelate
stories.description:
By Masereka Peter
The Bishop of the Diocese of Kasese, Rt. Rev. Francis Aquirinus Kibira Kambale, has called for renewed commitment among parents to take responsibility for the holistic formation of children, describing the family as the foundation upon which moral, spiritual, social and intellectual values are built
In an interview ahead of the annual Mbarara Ecclesiastical Province Kampala Residents Association (MEPA) pilgrimage at the Uganda Martyrs Catholic Shrine in Namugongo celebrated on Sunday 08th Nov 2026 animated by Hoima Catholic Diocese, Bishop Kibira emphasised that the family, which the Catholic Church describes as the Domestic Church, plays a fundamental role in shaping children's character, faith and behaviour.
He noted that although schools provide formal education and the Church offers spiritual guidance, the family remains the first environment where children learn values and develop their understanding of life.
Below are excerpts from the interview.
Question: Your Lordship, what is the role of the family in the holistic formation of a child?
Bishop Kibira: The family occupies a very central position in the formation of a child. In the Catholic Church, we describe the family as the Domestic Church because it is the first place where the salvific work of God is experienced, lived and transmitted.
The family is not merely a social institution but a sacred environment where children learn love, respect, responsibility, forgiveness and the fear of God.
Parents have a special responsibility, through the Sacrament of Holy Matrimony, to create an environment characterised by mutual respect, self-giving love, prayer and awareness of God's presence.
A child is not born fully formed; formation is a continuous process. Schools educate, the Church evangelises, but the family has the primary responsibility of forming the child.
Question: Why do you consider the family the first school of human and Christian values?
Bishop Kibira: The family is where a child first encounters life and begins to understand relationships, discipline, respect and responsibility.
Traditionally, African societies had strong communal structures in which parents, grandparents, extended family members and community elders actively participated in raising children.
A child belonged not only to the biological parents but also to the wider community, which shared responsibility for his or her upbringing.
This communal approach helped children grow up with a sense of belonging and responsibility towards others.
The Second Vatican Council also recognises the family as the first school of human and Christian values. Therefore, parents must understand that the responsibility of forming children cannot be transferred entirely to teachers, priests or other institutions.
Question: What challenges are currently affecting the role of families in the upbringing of children, particularly in Uganda?
Bishop Kibira: There are several challenges affecting families today. One of the major concerns is poverty, which has forced many parents to spend most of their time looking for income, sometimes leaving children without adequate parental guidance.
We are also witnessing absentee parenting, child labour, domestic violence and conflicts between couples. These situations negatively affect the emotional, psychological and spiritual development of children.
Another challenge is the breakdown of extended-family structures that traditionally supported parents in raising children.
We must also recognise the influence of digital technology, excessive use of mobile phones, secularism and other emerging social pressures, which expose children to inappropriate content, substance abuse and early sexual activities.
When children grow up in environments where they feel neglected or emotionally insecure, their education, moral development and spiritual growth are likely to suffer.
Question: What practical measures can parents take to address these challenges and improve the formation of their children?
Bishop Kibira: Parents must first reclaim their responsibility as the primary educators of their children.
They need to create time for their families despite the economic demands of modern life. It is important for parents to communicate openly with their children, understand their challenges and guide them through the different stages of growth.
Family prayer is equally important. Parents should make it a habit to pray together, read the Bible as a family and participate actively in the sacramental life of the Church.
They should also practise mutual respect, make important family decisions together and resolve disagreements peacefully.
Children learn more from what parents do than what they simply tell them. Therefore, parents must become good examples through their conduct, relationships and commitment to Christian values.
Question: What contribution can Church movements and family apostolate groups, such as the Cana Apostolate, make towards strengthening families?
Bishop Kibira: Family apostolate movements have an important role in helping couples understand and fulfil their responsibilities within marriage and family life.
Movements such as the Cana Apostolate provide opportunities for couples to accompany one another, strengthen their marriages and address challenges affecting their families.
Through marriage enrichment programmes, family discussions, prayer and spiritual formation, couples are encouraged to communicate effectively, make decisions together and develop better ways of resolving conflicts.
These movements also remind parents that they are not alone in facing family challenges. The Church is ready to accompany them through pastoral guidance and spiritual support.
When couples strengthen their relationships, children benefit from growing up in peaceful, loving and supportive homes.
Question: How can the Church and families work together to protect children from domestic violence and other forms of abuse?
Bishop Kibira: The Church and families must work together because the protection of children is a shared responsibility.
Parents must ensure that their homes are places of safety, love and understanding rather than fear, violence and intimidation.
Domestic violence is particularly harmful because children who grow up witnessing violence between their parents may experience emotional insecurity and develop unhealthy attitudes towards relationships.
The Church, through its pastoral programmes and family apostolate movements, must continue educating couples about peaceful coexistence, responsible parenthood, forgiveness and respect for human dignity.
We must encourage couples to seek guidance whenever they encounter challenges instead of allowing disagreements to develop into violence.
Question: What message do you have for parents who believe that providing school fees, food and other material necessities is enough to raise responsible children?
Bishop Kibira: Providing material necessities is important, but parenting goes beyond meeting the physical needs of children.
Children also need emotional support, spiritual guidance, moral instruction and the presence of their parents in their daily lives.
A parent may provide everything materially but still fail in the responsibility of forming a child if there is no communication, love, guidance and positive example.
Parents should remember that children need their time and attention. They must know what their children are doing, the friends they associate with, the challenges they face and the values they are developing.
We should not leave the responsibility of raising children entirely to schools, domestic workers or other people.
Question: Finally, what is your message to Ugandan families regarding the future of children and society?
Bishop Kibira: My appeal to all families is to rediscover the importance of the family as the Domestic Church.
Parents should embrace their vocation through the Sacrament of Holy Matrimony and make their homes centres of prayer, love, reconciliation and healing.
Family life will not always be without challenges. There will be moments of suffering, disagreements and difficulties, but couples must learn to face these experiences together, guided by their Christian faith and the example of Jesus Christ.
When parents live their faith genuinely, forgive one another and create an atmosphere of open communication, they give their children a strong foundation for life.
The future of the Church and society depends greatly on how we raise our children today. We must therefore invest in their holistic formation so that they grow into responsible, compassionate and morally upright citizens who can contribute positively to the Church and the wider Ugandan society.
END

stories.title: KENYA: Kenyan Environmentalist Calls for Climate Justice, Shared Responsibility at COP31
stories.description:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
Following the ongoing United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, a Kenyan environmentalist has called on world leaders to put justice at the centre of climate action, warning that communities that did the least to cause the climate crisis should not be left to carry its heaviest burdens.
Ms. Ashley Kitisya, the Africa Regional Director at Laudato Si' Movement (LSM) and the organisation's representative at the summit, said the crisis goes beyond the environment.
The climate crisis is not only an environmental emergency. It is a question of justice, human dignity, and our shared responsibility to one another, Kitisya said and added, At COP31, governments, faith communities, and civil society must work together to turn commitments into concrete action, ensuring that those who have contributed least to the climate crisis are not left to bear its greatest burdens.
The Catholic climate movement, which opened its COP31 campaign on 9 November as the talks began, is urging governments to agree on concrete pathways away from coal, oil and gas, and to tax fossil-fuel profits to support affected communities. It also wants people living with the effects of climate change to have a real voice in the decisions that shape their lives.
According to the LSM regional director, a fair transition must deliver affordable renewable energy, protect workers and communities, and provide adequate grant-based finance for developing countries, rather than loans that deepen debt.
Ms. Kitisya says wealthier nations must move first and fastest, while polluters, not vulnerable households, bear the costs of the shift away from fossil fuels.
Through its Europe Be Faithful for Our Common Home campaign, LSM and its partners are pressing European leaders to back their climate pledges with policies and financing that advance a just transition both at home and abroad.
The organisation is also calling for reform of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) process to safeguard meaningful participation by civil society, strengthen transparency and accountability, and shield climate policymaking from fossil-fuel interests.
Ms. Kitisya stressed that lasting change depends on cooperation, saying, At Laudato Si' Movement, we believe that real change happens when we build strong partnerships, bring communities together, and work toward a common purpose, she said.
LSM is taking part in COP31 to ensure the voices and experiences of affected communities are heard in decision-making spaces, working alongside faith-based organisations and civil society partners to link global commitments with local realities.
Through the Laudato Si' Action Platform and Peoples' Determined Contributions, the movement is also showcasing community-led initiatives that show how local action can contribute to global climate goals, while demanding greater ambition and accountability from governments.
To negotiators, Ms. Kitisya says the movement encourages listening to affected communities, engaging in genuine dialogue, and turning commitments into measurable action.
The call from Antalya is being echoed on the ground in several countries, including Kenya.
In Nairobi, LSM is working with 350.org, JPIC Franciscans Africa, Greenpeace, Climate Action Network (CAN) Eastern Africa, the Kenya Wildlife Service and the Catholic University of Eastern Africa (CUEA) to hold a COP31 People's March and Town Hall on 14 November. Organisers say the event will create space for public dialogue, community participation and collective calls for climate action.
On the same day, Laudato Si' Animators in Ireland and France are joining climate marches alongside civil society groups to demand a just transition away from fossil fuels.
In France, LSM has partnered with the French Bishops' Conference on a ready-to-use toolkit to help communities organise prayer vigils throughout the summit. In Canada, together with For the Love of Creation, the movement backed Candles for COP31, an online prayer vigil for climate justice on 9 November, followed by an in-person gathering in Toronto on 12 November.
COP31 brings together governments, civil society and other stakeholders to negotiate the next steps in the global response to climate change.

stories.title: Self-sensing artificial muscles made with graphene fibers play piano and move robotic eyes
stories.description: Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania have developed artificial muscle fibers that sense their own contraction state and hold intermediate positions on demand, a capability that has largely eluded soft actuators. The fibers, called CoilLCE, combine a liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) with multilayer graphene powder and an ultrathin copper coil embedded along the fiber’s length, and translate electrical signals into muscle-like motion. Ziyun Zhang, co-lead author of the study, with the robotic eyes and hand used to demonstrate the CoilLCE artificial muscles. Image credit: Penn EngineeringThe fibers contain just 0.25 wt.% graphene. At that loading the composite reached a toughness of 632 MJ/m³, more than three times the 192 MJ/m³ of a pure LCE fiber, and its stiffness decreased rather than increased, bringing it closer to the Young’s modulus of skeletal muscle, 0.1 to 0.3 MPa. The researchers attribute this to graphene sheets acting as physical barriers between oligomer chains, lowering the effective crosslink density without disrupting the liquid crystal alignment that the actuation depends on. At 0.75 wt.% the alignment was substantially impaired, and both actuation strain and breaking stress declined. The reduced stiffness also lowers the force a passively stretched fiber exerts against its contracting partner. In antagonistic pairs the graphene-loaded fibers reached an actuation strain of 16.1%, compared with 11.2% for pure LCE, an improvement of about 44%. The graphene also improved the uniformity of heating along the fiber.
